```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

rm(list = ls())
if (rstudioapi::isAvailable()) {
  setwd(dirname(rstudioapi::getActiveDocumentContext()$path))
}

out_dir <- "../../output/5_inference_final"
topic_path <- "../../input/topics/topic_labels.csv"
cov_dir <- "../../input/covariates"

fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
f1 <- function(x) ifelse(x < 0.1, sprintf("%.3f", x), sprintf("%.2f", x))
or3 <- function(m, l, u) sprintf("%s (%s-%s)", f1(m), f1(l), f1(u))
mech_names <- c(ER = "Emotional Reactions", IP = "Interpretations", EX = "Explorations")
llm_names <- c(gemini = "Gemini", openai = "OpenAI", grok = "Grok")
llm_cols <- c(Gemini = "#0072B2", OpenAI = "#D55E00", Grok = "#009E73")
CREDIBLE_PD <- 0.975
EXPLORATORY_BELOW <- 0.05
is_cred <- function(pd, lcl, ucl) pd > CREDIBLE_PD & (lcl > 1 | ucl < 1)

# --- data size and raw rates (same weighting as the models) ---------------
cells <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "qc_filter_and_balance.csv"))
n_threads <- n_distinct(cells$post_id)
n_synth <- sum(cells$original_n)
n_real <- sum(distinct(cells, post_id, real_count)$real_count)

raw <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "inference_results.csv")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(response_post) & response_post != "")
rc <- raw %>% filter(source == "real") %>% count(post_id, name = "real_count")
raw <- raw %>%
  left_join(rc, by = "post_id") %>% mutate(real_count = coalesce(real_count, 0L)) %>%
  group_by(post_id, model, method) %>% mutate(cell_n = n()) %>% ungroup() %>%
  mutate(w = ifelse(source == "real", 1, pmin(1, real_count / cell_n))) %>% filter(w > 0)
raw_rates <- raw %>%
  mutate(who = ifelse(source == "real", "Real clinicians", paste("AI:", llm_names[model]))) %>%
  group_by(who) %>%
  summarise(ER = weighted.mean(ER_label >= 1, w), IP = weighted.mean(IP_label >= 1, w),
            EX = weighted.mean(EX_label >= 1, w), .groups = "drop")
raw_all <- raw %>% group_by(source) %>%
  summarise(ER = weighted.mean(ER_label >= 1, w), IP = weighted.mean(IP_label >= 1, w),
            EX = weighted.mean(EX_label >= 1, w), .groups = "drop")
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
pct1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)

# --- topics ---------------------------------------------------------------
topics <- read.csv(topic_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
lookup <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_topic_lookup.csv"))
n_topics <- nrow(lookup)
n_threads_in <- sum(lookup$n_threads)
n_expl <- sum(lookup$exploratory)
n_cancer <- sum(tolower(topics$cancer_relevant) == "true", na.rm = TRUE)
n_cancer_na <- sum(!tolower(topics$cancer_relevant) %in% c("true", "false"))
sev_raw <- read.csv(file.path(cov_dir, "severity.csv"))
n_sev_na <- sum(is.na(sev_raw$severity_score))

# --- results --------------------------------------------------------------
conv <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_topic_convergence.csv"))
sdp <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_topic_sd_summary.csv"))
sdl <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_llm_sd_summary.csv"))
canc <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_topic_cancer_moderation.csv"))
covs <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_covariate_effects.csv"))
sevm <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_severity_moderation.csv"))
tp <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_topic_gap_by_topic.csv"))
tl <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_topic_by_llm.csv"))
dl <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "v2_llm_differences_by_topic.csv"))

avg <- tp %>% filter(is.na(topic))
bt <- tp %>% filter(!is.na(topic)) %>% mutate(credible = is_cred(shift_pd, shift_lcl, shift_ucl))
avg_llm <- tl %>% filter(is.na(topic)) %>% mutate(who_n = llm_names[who])
btl <- tl %>% filter(!is.na(topic)) %>% mutate(credible = is_cred(shift_pd, shift_lcl, shift_ucl), who_n = llm_names[who])
dl <- dl %>% mutate(credible = is_cred(shift_ratio_pd, shift_ratio_lcl, shift_ratio_ucl))

gap_of <- function(df, m, w = NULL) { r <- df[df$mechanism == m & (if (is.null(w)) TRUE else df$who == w), ]; stopifnot(nrow(r) == 1); r }
sev_cred <- sevm %>% mutate(credible = is_cred(sev_pd, sev_lcl, sev_ucl))
```

# In short

Earlier analyses showed that AI-written replies to patient questions show
less empathy than real clinician replies. This report asks **when** the gap is
larger or smaller. We tested four things that might change it: the medical
topic of the question, *which* AI model wrote the reply, how severe the
patient's problem is, and whether cancer is involved.

- **The gap depends strongly on the kind of empathy.** On average, AI replies
  are much less likely than real ones to react emotionally (odds ratio
  `r f1(gap_of(avg, "ER")$gap_or)`) or to explore the patient's experience
  (`r f1(gap_of(avg, "EX")$gap_or)`). For interpretations the average is closer to
  parity (`r f1(gap_of(avg, "IP")$gap_or)`).
- **The three AI models differ a lot, and for interpretations they differ in
  direction.** Grok's replies show interpretation *more* often than real
  clinicians' (odds ratio `r f1(gap_of(avg_llm, "IP", "grok")$gap_or)`); Gemini's
  (`r f1(gap_of(avg_llm, "IP", "gemini")$gap_or)`) and OpenAI's
  (`r f1(gap_of(avg_llm, "IP", "openai")$gap_or)`) show it less often.
  Averaging over models hides this.
- **Topic matters, but modestly and mostly for explorations.** The gap varies
  across the `r n_topics` topics for all three kinds of empathy
  (`r sum(bt$credible)` topic-level differences are credible), but the pattern
  is topic-specific rather than one topic standing out everywhere.
  Dermatology is the clearest case: AI explores relatively *more* there, and
  reacts emotionally relatively *less*.
- **Topic effects are mostly shared across models.** Only
  `r sum(dl$credible)` of the model-versus-model comparisons within a topic are
  credible, both for explorations.
- **Severity matters for interpretations.** The more severe the problem, the
  more AI replies catch up with real ones on interpretations, for all three
  models. For emotional reactions this holds for Gemini and OpenAI only; for
  explorations we find no effect.
- **Cancer-related questions shift the gap in opposite directions for
  interpretations (AI relatively better) and explorations (AI relatively
  worse).**

Everything here describes what automatic classifiers detect in text, and the
topic labels are themselves machine-made and imperfect (see
Section \@ref(caveats)).

# The study in plain terms

## The data

Each item is a patient question posted on Reddit's r/AskDocs. For each of the
`r fmt(n_threads)` threads we have the replies of real, verified clinicians
(`r fmt(n_real)` replies) and replies written by three AI models (Gemini,
OpenAI, Grok) given the same post, each under three prompting strategies
(`r fmt(n_synth)` AI replies in total). Prompting strategy is a nuisance factor
here: we keep the nine model-by-strategy combinations apart in the models
but report results per AI model.

## What was measured

Three classifiers, trained on the EPITOME framework of empathy in text-based
support, rated every reply on three kinds of empathy:

- **Emotional reaction (ER):** expressing warmth, concern or sympathy
  ("I'm sorry you're dealing with this").
- **Interpretation (IP):** showing an understanding of what the patient is
  feeling or experiencing ("it sounds like this has been worrying you").
- **Exploration (EX):** probing the patient's experience with follow-up
  questions ("how long has this been going on?").

Each is rated none, weak or strong. Replies with any empathy are
uncommon, so we ask a yes/no question: *does this reply show this kind of
empathy at all?* Table \@ref(tab:raw) gives the raw rates, adjusted so that
a thread's AI replies carry no more total weight than its real replies (see
"Making a fair comparison").

```{r raw}
raw_rates %>%
  mutate(across(c(ER, IP, EX), pct1)) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("", "Emotional reaction", "Interpretation", "Exploration"),
        align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
        caption = "Share of replies showing each kind of empathy (weighted).")
```

## The four moderators

A *moderator* is a variable that changes the size of an effect; here, the
real-vs-AI gap. We examined four.

1. **Topic.** A language model read each opening post and assigned one of
   17 medical disciplines (taxonomy from Chan et al., 2025). The label belongs
   to the thread, so a reply to a skin question is a "dermatology" reply
   whether a clinician or an AI wrote it. We merged some related disciplines
   (cardiology with pulmonology, dentistry with otolaryngology, neurology with
   ophthalmology, haematology/immunology with infectious diseases) and left out
   the two catch-all labels ("Medical; other", "Nonmedical"), leaving
   `r n_topics` topics and `r fmt(n_threads_in)` threads (Table \@ref(tab:topics)).
   `r n_expl` topic (Neoplasms) is small (under 5% of threads); it stays in the
   analysis but is flagged as exploratory.
2. **Which AI model** wrote the reply: does a topic affect Gemini, OpenAI and
   Grok differently?
3. **Cancer relevance.** A language-model flag for threads where cancer is
   involved (`r fmt(n_cancer)` threads; `r n_cancer_na` threads without a flag
   are dropped from this analysis only).
4. **Severity.** A 1-4 triage score for how serious the patient's problem is,
   from a collaborator's rating of each post. `r fmt(n_sev_na)` threads have no
   usable score (almost all rated "not applicable"); we do not treat these as low
   severity but give them their own indicator.

```{r topics}
lookup %>%
  arrange(desc(n_threads)) %>%
  mutate(share = pct1(share), n_threads = fmt(n_threads),
         exploratory = ifelse(exploratory, "yes", "")) %>%
  select(topic_label, n_threads, share, exploratory) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Topic", "Threads", "Share of all threads", "Exploratory (< 5%)"),
        align = c("l", "r", "r", "c"),
        caption = "The topics used in the analysis.")
```

## Other variables we controlled for

A collaborator proposed several thread-level variables. All models adjust for
them: who the post is about (the poster or someone else), the patient's age and
sex where stated, severity, and whether the first responder's declared
specialty matches the topic of the post (real replies only, since the AI
has no specialty). Missing values are coded with their own indicator rather
than guessed. Because these variables belong to the thread, and each thread
already has its own baseline in the models, they can only change the real-vs-AI
gap if we ask them to; severity is the one we tested that way. For the others
we report the effects on how often replies show empathy at all
(Section \@ref(res-cov)).

## Making a fair comparison

- **Replies in a thread are not independent.** A frightening question may draw
  empathy from everyone. Each thread has its own baseline in the model
  (a random intercept), so the comparison of real and AI replies is made
  *within* threads.
- **AI models wrote more replies than there were real ones.** If a thread
  has 2 real replies and a model wrote 8, each of its 8 replies counts for
  1/4, so both sides carry equal weight. This uses all the data and avoids
  the arbitrariness of randomly discarding replies. Reported intervals are
  approximate under this scheme.

## How to read the numbers

- **Odds ratio (OR).** The odds of a reply showing empathy are
  P/(1-P). The *gap* is the AI-to-real ratio of these odds *within the same
  thread*: below 1 means AI is less likely to show empathy, 0.5 means half the
  odds, above 1 means more likely. Because the comparison is within threads,
  these ratios are more extreme than the raw percentages in
  Table \@ref(tab:raw) would suggest.
- **Shift.** How much a moderator multiplies the gap relative to its average.
  For a topic: shift 1.3 means the gap is 1.3 times the average gap in that
  topic. If the average gap is below 1, a shift above 1 therefore means the AI
  is *closer to* real replies than average there.
- **95% credible interval.** The range that holds the true value with 95%
  probability given the data and model (a Bayesian analogue of a confidence
  interval).
- **pd (probability of direction).** The posterior probability that the effect
  has the sign we report. It is not a p-value. We call a result **credible**
  when pd exceeds 0.975 *and* the interval excludes 1.
- **Partial pooling.** Topic effects are treated like random effects:
  topics with plenty of threads get mostly their own estimate, topics with few
  are pulled toward the average. This guards against over-reading small topics
  and is why we apply no separate multiple-comparison correction.

# What to keep in mind {#caveats}

- **Topic labels are noisy.** The labelling model agrees with a 200-post
  reference set about 77% of the time, and the reference was itself built
  largely by language models. Roughly one label in four may be off. Noise in a
  grouping variable blurs real differences, so a missing topic effect is weaker
  evidence than it looks, and detected ones are probably underestimates.
- **Topic comes from the post, not the reply.** A reply that wanders off topic
  keeps the post's label.
- **Many comparisons, partial protection.** We look at
  `r nrow(bt)` pooled topic shifts and `r nrow(btl)` model-specific ones. Pooling
  limits false alarms, but around one in forty estimates can look credible by
  chance. Treat individual topics as leads, not conclusions, especially the
  exploratory topic.
- **Models, not strategies.** A topic shift is shared by an AI model's three
  prompting strategies. Whether strategies differ is not tested here.
- **Classifiers, not people.** All results describe what the classifiers
  detect.
- **Severity and specialty match are observational covariates.** Severity is
  a rating of the post; specialty match is partly a choice by whoever answers.
  We report associations, not causes.
- **Subsampling check pending.** A sensitivity analysis that randomly subsamples
  AI replies instead of weighting them is planned.

# Results {#results}

## Model checks

```{r conv-text}
model_names <- c(C2_topic_gap = "pooled topic model", D2_cancer = "cancer model",
                 E_topic_by_llm = "topic-by-model model", F_severity = "severity model")
bad <- conv[!conv$converged, ]
conv_msg <- if (nrow(bad) == 0) {
  sprintf("All %d fits met the convergence criteria (largest max Rhat %.4f, smallest effective-sample-size ratio %.3f, no divergent transitions).",
          nrow(conv), max(conv$max_rhat), min(conv$min_neff_ratio))
} else {
  sprintf("%d of %d fits met every convergence criterion. The exception%s: %s.",
          sum(conv$converged), nrow(conv), ifelse(nrow(bad) > 1, "s", ""),
          paste(vapply(seq_len(nrow(bad)), function(k) {
            r <- bad[k, ]
            sprintf("%s, %s (%s)", mech_names[[r$mechanism]], model_names[[r$model]],
                    paste(c(if (r$max_rhat >= 1.01) sprintf("max Rhat %.4f", r$max_rhat),
                            if (r$min_neff_ratio <= 0.1) sprintf("effective-sample-size ratio %.3f", r$min_neff_ratio),
                            if (isTRUE(r$divergent_transitions > 0)) sprintf("%d divergent transitions", r$divergent_transitions)),
                          collapse = ", "))
          }, character(1)), collapse = "; "))
}
```

`r conv_msg` Fits that initially fell short were rerun with twice as many
iterations (Methods); this did not change which effects are credible.

## The average gap, and how much it varies by topic

Table \@ref(tab:sd) shows the average gap and how much it moves from topic to
topic. "Spread" is the standard deviation of the topic shifts on the log-odds
scale; a spread of 0.44 means a typical topic multiplies the gap by about
$e^{0.44} \approx 1.55$ (or divides it by that).

```{r sd}
sd_slope <- sdp %>% filter(parameter == "topic_slope_sd")
tab <- avg %>%
  transmute(mechanism, avg_gap = or3(gap_or, gap_lcl, gap_ucl)) %>%
  left_join(sd_slope %>% transmute(mechanism, spread = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f-%.2f)", median, lcl, ucl),
                                   factor = sprintf("x%.2f", exp(median))), by = "mechanism") %>%
  mutate(mechanism = mech_names[mechanism])
kable(tab, col.names = c("Empathy type", "Average gap, OR (95% CrI)",
                         "Spread across topics, SD (95% CrI)", "Typical factor"),
      align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Average real-vs-AI gap (all AI replies pooled) and its variation across topics.")
```

`r sprintf("The spread's lower bound is clearly above zero (above 0.05) for %d of %d kinds of empathy", sum(sd_slope$lcl > 0.05), nrow(sd_slope))`,
so topic does change the gap. The effect is largest for explorations. Figure
\@ref(fig:forest) shows each topic's gap; filled points are topics whose shift
from the average is credible.

```{r forest, fig.width=9, fig.height=6.5, fig.cap="Real-vs-AI gap by topic (odds ratio, log scale; below 1 = AI less likely to show empathy). Filled points: credible shift from the average. Starred: under 5% of threads (exploratory). Dashed line: no gap; dotted red line: average over topics."}
plot_df <- bt %>%
  mutate(mechanism = factor(mech_names[mechanism], levels = unname(mech_names)),
         label = paste0(topic_label, ifelse(exploratory, " *", "")),
         label = factor(label, levels = unique(label[order(n_threads)])))
avg_df <- avg %>% mutate(mechanism = factor(mech_names[mechanism], levels = unname(mech_names)))
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = gap_or, y = label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(data = avg_df, aes(xintercept = gap_or), linetype = "dotted", colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = gap_lcl, xmax = gap_ucl), height = 0, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_point(aes(fill = credible), shape = 21, size = 2.6, colour = "black") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "black", `FALSE` = "white"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~mechanism, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Gap: odds ratio, AI vs. real (95% credible interval)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

`r sum(bt$credible)` of the `r nrow(bt)` topic shifts are credible
(Table \@ref(tab:credible)). For Emotional Reactions and Explorations the AI trails real replies in
every topic and the topic only changes by how much. For Interpretations the AI
is on par with or ahead of real replies in some topics (cardiopulmonary,
neurologic and visual, and musculoskeletal); in none of them does the
interval lie clearly above 1, with musculoskeletal the closest.

```{r credible}
cr <- bt %>% filter(credible) %>%
  arrange(match(mechanism, names(mech_names)), desc(n_threads)) %>%
  transmute(mechanism = mech_names[mechanism],
            topic = paste0(topic_label, ifelse(exploratory, " *", "")),
            threads = n_threads,
            gap = or3(gap_or, gap_lcl, gap_ucl),
            shift = or3(shift_or, shift_lcl, shift_ucl),
            pd = sprintf("%.3f", shift_pd),
            read = ifelse(shift_or > 1, "AI closer to real than average", "AI further from real than average"))
kable(cr, col.names = c("Empathy type", "Topic", "Threads", "Gap, OR (95% CrI)", "Shift, OR (95% CrI)", "pd", "Reading"),
      align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "l"),
      caption = "Topics whose gap credibly differs from the average (pooled AI replies).")
```

## Do the AI models differ in how topic matters? {#res-llm}

First, how big is each model's average gap (Table \@ref(tab:llmgap))? This is
the baseline the topic shifts are measured against.

```{r llmgap}
avg_llm %>%
  transmute(mechanism = mech_names[mechanism], model = who_n, gap = or3(gap_or, gap_lcl, gap_ucl)) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = gap) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Empathy type", "Gemini", "OpenAI", "Grok"), align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
        caption = "Average real-vs-AI gap per AI model, odds ratio (95% CrI).")
```

Second, does a topic shift the gap by a different amount for each model? If
the models responded to topics in the same way, their topic shifts would move
together. Table \@ref(tab:llmsd) gives the spread of topic shifts per model.

```{r llmsd}
sd_rows <- sdl %>% filter(grepl("^topic_slope_sd_", parameter)) %>%
  mutate(model = c(gem = "Gemini", opn = "OpenAI", grk = "Grok")[sub("topic_slope_sd_", "", parameter)],
         txt = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f-%.2f)", median, lcl, ucl)) %>%
  select(mechanism, model, txt) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = txt) %>%
  mutate(mechanism = mech_names[mechanism])
kable(sd_rows[, c("mechanism", "Gemini", "OpenAI", "Grok")],
      col.names = c("Empathy type", "Gemini", "OpenAI", "Grok"), align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Spread of the topic shifts per AI model, SD on the log-odds scale (95% CrI).")
```

Topic matters for each model for explorations (spread about 0.5 for all three),
and less consistently for the other two kinds. The topic shifts of the
different models are mostly positively related (estimated correlations from
-0.1 to 0.55), but with 11 topics these correlations are very uncertain (every
interval includes zero), so we cannot say how closely the models track one
another.

Figure \@ref(fig:llmforest) shows each model's shift by topic.
`r sum(btl$credible)` of `r nrow(btl)` shifts are credible
(Table \@ref(tab:llmcred)).

```{r llmforest, fig.width=9.5, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Topic shift of the real-vs-AI gap by AI model (odds ratio, log scale). Above 1: gap smaller than that model's average in that topic; below 1: larger. Filled: credible. Starred topic: exploratory."}
pl <- btl %>%
  mutate(mechanism = factor(mech_names[mechanism], levels = unname(mech_names)),
         label = paste0(topic_label, ifelse(exploratory, " *", "")),
         label = factor(label, levels = unique(label[order(n_threads)])),
         who_n = factor(who_n, levels = unname(llm_names)))
ggplot(pl, aes(x = shift_or, y = label, colour = who_n, shape = credible)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = shift_lcl, xmax = shift_ucl), orientation = "y",
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), size = 0.35, linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 16, `FALSE` = 1), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = llm_cols, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~mechanism) +
  labs(x = "Shift in gap relative to the model's average (odds ratio, 95% CrI)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r llmcred}
crl <- btl %>% filter(credible) %>%
  arrange(match(mechanism, names(mech_names)), who_n, desc(n_threads)) %>%
  transmute(mechanism = mech_names[mechanism], model = who_n,
            topic = paste0(topic_label, ifelse(exploratory, " *", "")),
            gap = or3(gap_or, gap_lcl, gap_ucl), shift = or3(shift_or, shift_lcl, shift_ucl),
            pd = sprintf("%.3f", shift_pd))
kable(crl, col.names = c("Empathy type", "Model", "Topic", "Gap in topic, OR (95% CrI)", "Shift, OR (95% CrI)", "pd"),
      align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Model-specific topic shifts that are credible.")
```

Finally, do two models differ in how a topic affects them? We compared the
shifts of each pair of models in each topic (`r nrow(dl)` comparisons).
`r if (sum(dl$credible) == 0) "None is credible." else sprintf("%d %s credible:", sum(dl$credible), ifelse(sum(dl$credible) == 1, "is", "are"))`

```{r dcred, results='asis'}
dc <- dl %>% filter(credible) %>% arrange(match(mechanism, names(mech_names)))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(dc))) {
  r <- dc[i, ]
  cat(sprintf("- **%s, %s, %s%s:** shift ratio %s (pd %.3f).\n", mech_names[r$mechanism], r$pair, r$topic_label,
              ifelse(r$exploratory, " (exploratory topic)", ""),
              or3(r$shift_ratio_or, r$shift_ratio_lcl, r$shift_ratio_ucl), r$shift_ratio_pd))
}
```

A shift ratio above 1 means the first model gains more than the second in that
topic, relative to each model's own average. Such differences between models are
rare, so the topic effects are largely common to the models.

## Cancer-related threads

```{r cancer, results='asis'}
for (i in seq_len(nrow(canc))) {
  r <- canc[i, ]
  cred <- is_cred(r$shift_pd, r$shift_lcl, r$shift_ucl)
  cat(sprintf("- **%s:** gap %s in other threads, %s in cancer-related threads. %s\n",
              mech_names[r$mechanism], f1(r$gap_not_cancer_or),
              or3(r$gap_cancer_or, r$gap_cancer_lcl, r$gap_cancer_ucl),
              if (cred) sprintf("The gap is credibly %s in cancer-related threads (shift %s, pd %.3f), meaning the AI is relatively %s there.",
                                ifelse(r$shift_or > 1, "smaller", "larger"),
                                or3(r$shift_or, r$shift_lcl, r$shift_ucl), r$shift_pd,
                                ifelse(r$shift_or > 1, "better", "worse"))
              else sprintf("No credible difference (shift %s, pd %.3f).", or3(r$shift_or, r$shift_lcl, r$shift_ucl), r$shift_pd)))
}
```

The cancer flag is separate from the "Neoplasms" topic, which is smaller and
only includes posts where a clinician or test has raised the concern. A
borderline interval (one end near 1) is weak evidence.

## Severity {#res-sev}

If the real-vs-AI gap depends on how severe the problem is, a severity
effect on its own is not enough: it must differ between real and AI replies.
We tested this with an interaction between severity and being AI-written,
separately for each model. Each number in Table \@ref(tab:sev) is how
much the gap changes (multiplies) per additional severity level (the scale
runs 1-4). A value above 1 means AI replies catch up with real ones as severity
rises; below 1 means they fall further behind.

```{r sev}
sv <- sev_cred %>% filter(grepl("per severity", term)) %>%
  mutate(who = ifelse(who %in% names(llm_names), llm_names[who], "All AI (mean of the three)"),
         txt = paste0(or3(sev_or, sev_lcl, sev_ucl), ifelse(credible, " *", ""))) %>%
  select(mechanism, who, txt) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = mechanism, values_from = txt)
kable(sv[, c("who", "ER", "IP", "EX")],
      col.names = c("", mech_names[["ER"]], mech_names[["IP"]], mech_names[["EX"]]),
      align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Change in the real-vs-AI gap per severity level, factor (95% CrI). * = credible.")
```

For interpretations the gap shrinks with severity for all three models.
For emotional reactions this holds for Gemini and OpenAI but not Grok, and the
average over the three is borderline. For explorations severity does not
change the gap. Threads with no usable severity rating
(`r fmt(n_sev_na)` threads) differ strongly in their overall gap, but this
probably reflects what kind of post cannot be rated, so we do not interpret it.

## Other covariates {#res-cov}

Table \@ref(tab:cov) shows how the other thread characteristics relate to
whether replies (real and AI alike, except where noted) show empathy. These
effects apply to the baseline rate, not the gap. Age is per decade; severity
per level; each is relative to a reference level (first-person posts, female
patients, rated severity, undeclared specialty).

```{r cov}
cov_lab <- c(subjectthird_party = "Post is about someone else", subjectunknown = "Post subject unclear",
             age10 = "Age (per decade)", age_na = "Age not stated",
             sex3male = "Male (vs. female)", sex3unknown = "Sex not stated",
             sev_c = "Severity (per level)", sev_na = "Severity not rated",
             real_match = "Real reply: first responder's specialty matches topic",
             real_mismatch = "Real reply: first responder's specialty differs from topic")
cv <- covs %>% mutate(credible = is_cred(effect_pd, effect_lcl, effect_ucl),
                      txt = paste0(or3(effect_or, effect_lcl, effect_ucl), ifelse(credible, " *", "")),
                      term = cov_lab[term]) %>%
  select(term, mechanism, txt) %>% tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = mechanism, values_from = txt)
kable(cv[, c("term", "ER", "IP", "EX")],
      col.names = c("", mech_names[["ER"]], mech_names[["IP"]], mech_names[["EX"]]),
      align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Association of thread characteristics with showing empathy, odds ratio (95% CrI). * = credible.")
```

Briefly: more severe problems draw more empathy of all kinds from both real
and AI replies; posts about someone else draw more interpretation (OR about
2.4); the demographic variables have small effects
(a few reach credibility, such as age for interpretations). Real replies in threads
where the first responder declared a body-system specialty show less emotional
reaction and exploration than threads without a declared specialty,
whether or not the specialty matches the topic. This probably reflects how
specialists write, or who chooses to declare a specialty, rather than the
match itself.

# Methods {#methods}

## Data and outcomes

All `r fmt(n_real + n_synth)` rated replies from `r fmt(n_threads)` threads
are used, with no outlier exclusion and no subsampling. Synthetic replies come
from Gemini, OpenAI and Grok, each under three prompting strategies (DG, SAG,
SAGII), giving nine synthetic groups plus the real group. Empathy labels
(0/1/2) for ER, IP and EX come from three fine-tuned RoBERTa bi-encoder
classifiers following EPITOME. The binary outcome is `label >= 1`. For IP and
EX label 1 never occurs in these data, so this equals `label == 2`.

## Topics and covariates

Topic labels come from the collaborators' pipeline (`classify_topics.py`):
gemini-2.5-pro at temperature 0, one of 17 disciplines per opening post,
joined on `submission_id`. Production-model agreement with a 200-post reference
sample was 0.770 (agreement between the two LLM annotators who built it:
0.795, $\kappa$ = 0.779). Four merges: Pulmonology + Cardiovascular,
Dentistry + Otolaryngology, Ophthalmology + Neurology, Hematology and immunology
+ Infectious diseases. "Nonmedical" and "Medical; other" are excluded from the
topic models. Topics under 5% of all threads are flagged exploratory but kept.

Covariates (all thread-level): `subject` (first person / third party /
unknown); `age10` (age in decades, centred at the median; missing set to 0 with
indicator `age_na`); `sex3` (female / male / unknown); `sev_c` (severity 1-4,
centred at the mean; "not applicable" and blank set to 0 with indicator
`sev_na`); `real_match` and `real_mismatch` (1 for real replies when the first
responder declared a body-system specialty that matches / does not match the
merged topic, else 0; reference: no declared body-system specialty; 0 for all
synthetic replies). Not used: weight, height, BMI, race, smoking, drinking and
time to first response, following the collaborator's documentation (heavy or
topic-dependent missingness).

## Response weights

With $n_c$ synthetic replies in a (thread, model, method) cell and $r$ real
replies in the thread, real replies have weight 1 and synthetic ones
$w = \min(1, r / n_c)$. Weights are computed on all threads before topic
filtering. They enter the log-likelihood as multipliers (`brms`
`weights()`), so estimates target the average over random per-thread
subsampling but posterior intervals are approximate.

## Models

Fitted separately for ER, IP and EX; Bernoulli likelihood, logit link. For
reply $i$: $s_i$ indicates a synthetic reply, $s_{iL}$ a reply from model $L$
(Gemini, OpenAI, Grok), $\beta_{g(i)}$ the coefficient for its group,
$\mathbf{x}_i$ the covariates above, $\ell_i$ log reply length in words,
$t(i)$ its thread's topic and $p(i)$ the thread.

**C2 (pooled topic moderation).**
$$\operatorname{logit} P(y_i=1)=\alpha+\beta_{g(i)}+\mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\delta+\gamma\ell_i+u_{t(i)}+v_{t(i)}s_i+a_{p(i)}$$
with $(u_t,v_t)\sim\mathcal N(0,\Sigma)$, $a_p\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_p^2)$. A
topic's gap is the mean of the nine synthetic $\beta_g$ plus $v_t$ (the shift),
exponentiated.

**E (topic moderation per model).** Replace $v_{t}s_i$ by
$\sum_L v_{tL}s_{iL}$, with $(u_t,v_{t,\mathrm{gem}},v_{t,\mathrm{opn}},v_{t,\mathrm{grk}})\sim\mathcal N(0,\Sigma)$
and an LKJ(2) prior on the correlations. A model's gap in a topic is the mean of
its three $\beta_g$ plus $v_{tL}$. Differences between models are computed from
the draws (ratio of gap ORs, ratio of shift ORs).

**D2 (cancer).** No topic effects;
$\ldots+\eta c_{p(i)}+\theta s_ic_{p(i)}+\ldots$ with cancer flag $c$; $\theta$ is the moderation.

**F (severity).** Model C2 plus $\sum_L\lambda_L s_{iL}\,\mathrm{sev}_i+\kappa s_i\,\mathrm{sevNA}_i$. Since
severity is also a covariate, $\lambda_L$ is the *extra* change in model $L$'s gap per
severity level, over and above any effect of severity on real replies;
the pooled value is the mean of the three. Topic effects stay in the model so
severity does not stand in for topic.

## Priors, sampling, convergence

Fixed effects: Normal(0, 2.5). Intercept and thread SD: Student-$t$(3, 0, 2.5).
Topic SDs: Normal(0, 1), truncated at 0. `brms` with `cmdstanr`; 4 chains of
2,000 iterations (1,000 warmup), 4 threads per chain, `adapt_delta` = 0.95,
seed 20260101. A fit is accepted when max $\hat R<1.01$, minimum
effective-sample-size ratio $>0.1$ and there are no divergent transitions.
Seven fits that fell marginally short (cancer models for all three kinds
of empathy, severity models for ER and EX, pooled topic models for IP and EX)
were refitted with 4,000 iterations (1,000 warmup); the credible topic effects
were unchanged. The refit of the IP pooled topic model improved
$\hat R$ but still has divergent transitions (reported under Model checks),
as in our earlier topic analysis; the topic-level intercept SD for
interpretations is close to zero, which makes the sampler's job harder. Multithreaded summation makes draws non-reproducible from the seed
alone, so the saved fits (`models_bayesian/`) and the run metadata are the
reproducible artefacts.

## Reporting

Posterior median odds ratio, 95% highest-density interval and
$pd=\max\{P(\theta>0),P(\theta<0)\}$ on the log-odds scale. Credible: pd > 0.975
and the interval excludes 1. No frequentist multiplicity correction; topic
effects are partially pooled instead. Code: `3i_topic_llm_moderation_v2.R`.

## Limitations

- Misclassified topics attenuate moderation estimates; no correction applied.
- A topic effect is shared by a model's three strategies.
- With 11 topics, correlations between models' topic shifts are poorly
  determined, and topic-specific cells for single models are noisy.
- The cancer flag is a distinct construct from the Neoplasms topic.
- Specialty match and severity are observational; severity not-rated threads
  have a different gap, which we do not interpret.
- Weighted intervals are approximate.

# Outlook: do prompting strategies change the picture? {#outlook}

This report keeps the three prompting strategies (DG, SAG, SAGII) apart in
the models, but reports topic and severity effects per AI model, not per
strategy. Earlier analyses found that strategies often differ within a model
(mostly modestly, but about two-fold for some of Grok's emotional reactions and
explorations), far less than the differences between models. So strategy could
plausibly also change how topic and severity matter. We have not tested this.
The options, from most to least constrained:

1. **Topic and severity effects per strategy, pooled over models.** Separate
   severity interactions and topic shifts for DG, SAG and SAGII, each
   averaged over the three AI models. Three effects per topic, comparable in
   size to the per-model analysis here. The drawback is that strategies can
   behave differently in different models (as they do for Grok), which this
   version averages away.
2. **Severity per model-by-strategy group.** Nine severity interactions as
   ordinary fixed effects. Severity is one number per thread, so this is well
   determined and cheap.
3. **Topic shifts per group with a shared spread.** Each topic-by-group
   combination (11 topics x 9 groups) gets its own deviation, all drawn from a
   single common standard deviation. This is estimable, keeps all nine groups
   and tells us whether the topic effects vary by group at all.
4. **The full model: a separate topic shift for each of the nine groups, with
   their correlations.** This is not impossible to run, but the data cannot
   support it: it needs 55 covariance parameters estimated from 11 topics, the
   cells are sparse (for example about 2% of Grok's replies show exploration),
   and it would produce around 300 topic-by-group estimates per kind of
   empathy to sift through. The result would be mostly prior-driven.

Options 2 and 3 together are the closest feasible approximation to the full
question. Whatever is chosen should come after the planned subsampling
sensitivity check, since that determines how far the weighted intervals can be
trusted.
